solutions.check: bars rebuilt from the blog's numbered answers (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Short poem, second one beloved lassie returned?

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral for one
jo is Scots for a sweetheart; the lassie's beloved is one whose love is returned

explanation.surface: A short poem addressed to a second sweetheart who has come back.
explanation.walkthrough: JO is a Scots word for a sweetheart, as in Burns's 'John Anderson, my jo'. 'Returned' does not reverse anything here: the blog found it an odd addition, best read as love returned.
explanation.definitionFit: A sijo is a brief Korean verse form of three lines, so it is a short poem.

clue.text: Articulation she's damaged with disc inly

indicators.note: something damaged is knocked out of shape, so the letters are put in a new order

explanation.surface: A medical note: a joint of hers has been injured, with a disc damaged internally.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Damaged' shuffles SHES, DISC and INLY together. 'Inly' (inwardly) is a real if poetic word, so it reads as part of the surface rather than fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: Schindylesis is the anatomical term for a joint in which a ridge of one bone fits into a groove of another, a kind of articulation.

clue.text: Clerical collar to choke dignitary?

parts.note: to jam is to block or choke up
a pot, or big pot, is an important person

explanation.surface: A dog collar so tight it chokes some church dignitary.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags the slang 'pot' for a bigwig.
explanation.definitionFit: Jampot is slang for the high, round clerical collar, whose shape resembles a jam jar.

clue.text: E.g. Springboks, profligate, ditching leader before new series

indicators.note: ditching the leader means the first letter of the word is dropped

parts.note: a roué is a profligate, a dissolute man
S is an abbreviation for series

explanation.surface: A rugby squad, the Springboks, lose a dissolute captain before a new tour.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ditching leader' strips the R from ROUE to leave OUE. OU is South African slang for a man or fellow, and OUENS is one of its plurals; the Springboks are South Africa's rugby side.
explanation.definitionFit: The South African rugby players are an example of blokes, which is the slang plural meaning here.

clue.text: Knotted tense round bow of fine material

indicators.note: the jumbled letters go round, enclosing the other piece
something knotted is twisted and tangled, so the letters are jumbled

parts.note: an arc is a curve, a bow shape

explanation.surface: Knotting a bow from a length of fine cloth under tension.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bow' is a curve here, not a ribbon or a knot, despite 'Knotted' beside it; 'round' wraps the jumbled SENET about ARC.
explanation.definitionFit: Sarcenet is a thin, soft silk fabric used for linings, so it is a fine material.

clue.text: Gosh, look! Help has restricted that starchy deposit

indicators.note: to restrict is to hem in, so one piece is enclosed by the other

parts.note: aid means help
'my!' is an exclamation like 'gosh!'
lo is an old word for look or behold

explanation.surface: Someone exclaims in surprise that helping has held a starchy build-up in check.
explanation.definitionFit: Amyloid is a starch-like protein that builds up in tissues in some diseases, a waxy deposit named for its supposed starchiness.

clue.text: The old abjure measure dividing abandoned apparel

indicators.note: the measure splits the other word, sitting inside it
the word for apparel has abandoned its first two letters, an aphetic form

parts.note: array means fine clothing, apparel
an en is a printer's measure of width

explanation.surface: An old command to renounce some measure that has come between people and the clothes they discarded.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Abandoned' clips the word for apparel to RAY, Spenser's short form, which 'dividing' then splits with the printer's measure. 'The old' tells you the definition is archaic.
explanation.definitionFit: Renay is an obsolete word meaning to renounce or deny, so it is an archaic synonym of abjure.

clue.text: Suitable for a funeral, as one in embroidered lace

indicators.note: the first pieces are placed in the rearranged letters
embroidered means worked over and elaborated, signalling the letters are rearranged

parts.note: e.g. (for example) can stand for 'as', as in 'such as'
I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: Embroidered lace that suits a funeral, as a shroud might.
explanation.walkthrough: 'As' is a common crossword stand-in for EG, since 'such as' and 'for example' overlap; 'embroidered' gives ELAC, with EG and I put 'in' after its L.
explanation.definitionFit: Elegiac means mournful, in the manner of an elegy or lament, so it suits a funeral.

clue.text: Former novelty, not old clearly

parts.note: ne is an archaic word for not
well can mean clearly, as in 'well visible'

explanation.surface: Something new once is clearly not old.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Not old' looks like 'new', but it means 'not' in old English: NE.
explanation.definitionFit: Newell is an obsolete Spenserian word for a novelty or new thing, so 'former' marks it as archaic.

clue.text: I'll have read tome with note added, 'for correction'?

definitions.text: I'll have read tome with note added, 'for correction'?

indicators.note: letters sent for correction get put right and rearranged

explanation.surface: A proofreader promises to read the book and mark it for correction.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is the editor speaking: 'for correction' signals that READ TOME plus N are put right into a new order, which is just what such a person does.
explanation.definitionFit: An emendator is one who emends or corrects a text, which is what the speaker of the clue is doing.

clue.text: Irritable about art, name obscured, forming part of bequest

indicators.note: the first word goes about, enclosing the rest

parts.note: testy means irritable

indicators.note: obscured letters are muddled so they are no longer clear

explanation.surface: A tetchy heir complains that an artwork left in a will has its name hidden.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Obscured' muddles the middle words into AMENTAR, and 'about' has the word for irritable wrap round it. The surface's will and bequest point straight at the answer's meaning.
explanation.definitionFit: Testamentary describes what belongs to a will, so items forming part of a bequest are testamentary.

clue.text: Much ale led, when drunk… to such an end for Marlowe?

indicators.note: drunk letters stagger about, so they are rearranged

explanation.surface: Heavy drinking led to a violent death, as for the playwright Marlowe.
explanation.walkthrough: 'When drunk' rearranges MUCH ALE LED. Christopher Marlowe was reportedly stabbed in a tavern brawl.
explanation.definitionFit: Chaud-mellé is a sudden fight in hot blood, or a killing in such a brawl, which is how Marlowe died.

clue.text: Ray: unpretentious name

parts.note: homely means simple and unpretentious

explanation.surface: Someone called Ray has a plain, unpretentious name.
explanation.walkthrough: Ray looks like a man's name, but it is the fish.
explanation.definitionFit: The homelyn is the spotted ray, a fish of the skate family.

clue.text: Fifty members of flock somewhere in E. Sussex

parts.note: L is the Roman numeral for fifty
ewes are female sheep in a flock

explanation.surface: Fifty sheep from a flock grazing somewhere in East Sussex.
explanation.walkthrough: Lewes is the county town of East Sussex, in southern England.
explanation.definitionFit: Lewes is a town in East Sussex, so it is an example of a place there.

clue.text: Self-styled idiots staggering round old nursing home

indicators.note: the rearranged letters go round the other piece
staggering suggests reeling about, so the letters are mixed up

parts.note: san is a dated short form of sanatorium

explanation.surface: Some self-proclaimed experts reel drunkenly around a retirement home.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Staggering' scrambles the idiots into SOIDIT, which goes 'round' the dated short form of sanatorium. The answer is a French phrase meaning 'calling oneself'.
explanation.definitionFit: Soi-disant is used for a so-called or self-proclaimed person, one claiming a title without warrant.

clue.text: Ringing factory about info

indicators.note: the first word is placed about the second, enclosing it

parts.note: a plant is a factory
gen is slang for information

explanation.surface: A factory phones round for information.
explanation.walkthrough: 'About' has the factory word enclose the slang for information; gen is British slang. 'Ringing' looks like a telephone call but is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Plangent describes a loud, resonant, often mournful sound, like a ringing bell.

clue.text: Texan's necktie made with new Scottish woolstuff?

parts.note: oose is Scots for fluff or nap from wool

explanation.surface: A cowboy's tie made of new Scottish wool.
explanation.walkthrough: A 'necktie party' is old Wild West slang for a hanging, so a Texan's necktie is the hangman's rope.
explanation.definitionFit: Chambers records necktie as American slang for a hangman's rope, the loop that goes round the neck.

clue.text: Daughter (not the first)? A girl

indicators.note: the first letter of the word is left off

parts.note: a daughter is a child

explanation.surface: Wondering whether a daughter who is not the eldest is a girl.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Not the first' looks like it means a younger daughter, but it removes the first letter of the word for offspring, leaving HILD. 'A' then follows as written.
explanation.definitionFit: Hilda is a girl's name, so it is an example of a girl.

clue.text: Words of old song hold up e.g. Guebre

parts.note: dit is an old word for a ditty, the words of a song
a heist is a hold-up, a robbery

explanation.surface: An old song tells of a robbery by a Zoroastrian.
explanation.walkthrough: A Guebre is a Zoroastrian fire-worshipper; Zoroastrianism sets two gods, good and evil, against each other.
explanation.definitionFit: A ditheist believes in two gods, and a Zoroastrian is an example of such a dualist believer.

clue.text: Monkey before being eclipsed by Homo sapiens?

indicators.note: eclipsed means hidden behind, so this piece goes inside the other

parts.note: Homo sapiens is the scientific name for a human
an is taken as an old word for before, the split the blog gives too

explanation.surface: The monkey came first, before humans overshadowed it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Being eclipsed by' means hidden inside Homo sapiens' everyday name. The surface nods at evolution; Hanuman is also the monkey god of Hindu myth.
explanation.definitionFit: The hanuman is the entellus langur, a sacred Indian monkey named after the monkey god.

clue.text: Take into something larger amount kept in by cork mostly

indicators.note: the amount is held inside the other piece
mostly means all but the last letter

parts.note: suber is the botanical term for cork tissue
a sum is an amount

explanation.surface: A sum of money is stowed away in something larger, sealed in by a cork.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mostly' trims SUBER to SUBE, and SUM is 'kept in by' it. Suber is the botanist's word for cork.
explanation.definitionFit: To subsume is to include something within a larger class or group.

clue.text: Fruit to satisfy once fed to the old man

indicators.note: food fed to someone goes inside them

parts.note: pa is an informal word for one's father
apay is an archaic verb meaning to satisfy or repay

explanation.surface: Giving Dad some fruit to keep him happy.
explanation.definitionFit: The papaya is a tropical fruit, also called the pawpaw.

clue.text: Does it describe end of line for angler at being taken in by an ignoramus?

definitions.text: Does it describe end of line for angler

indicators.note: taken in means held inside, so this word sits within the others

parts.note: an is the indefinite article, giving A
a dunce is an ignorant person

explanation.surface: Asking whether a fishing line ends with something a fool might fall for.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Being taken in by' places 'at' inside 'an ignoramus' read as article plus fool. The end of an angler's line is the hook, which the definition asks you to picture.
explanation.definitionFit: Aduncate means hooked or bent like a hook, so it describes a fish-hook.

clue.text: Primate packing little drink: 'I've only one case'

indicators.note: to pack something is to hold it inside

parts.note: an ape is a primate
a tot is a small measure of spirits

explanation.surface: An ape with a drink in its suitcase claims to have just one bag.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Packing' has APE hold TOT. 'Case' is grammatical here, not luggage.
explanation.definitionFit: An aptote is a noun with no case inflections, so in effect it has only one form.

clue.text: Bit of old Chinese money pocketed by Mongolian gent

indicators.note: pocketed means tucked inside, so the letters lie within these words

parts.note: the letters run across the end of Mongolian and the start of gent

explanation.surface: A Mongolian man pockets an old Chinese coin.
explanation.definitionFit: The liang was an old Chinese unit of weight, also called the tael, used as money in silver.

clue.text: Car going over second of potholes lost exhaust

parts.note: a Ford is a make of car

indicators.note: the second letter of the word that follows is the one taken

parts.note: second letter of potholes

explanation.surface: A car drives over potholes and loses its exhaust pipe.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Second of' takes the O of potholes after FORD. 'Exhaust' looks like the car part but it is a verb, and 'lost' marks it as a word no longer used.
explanation.definitionFit: Fordo is an archaic verb meaning to destroy or wear out, as in 'fordone' meaning tired out.

clue.text: Top points? In wrestling tots this perhaps

definitions.text: Top points? In wrestling tots this perhaps

indicators.note: wrestling suggests a tussle, so the letters are thrown about and rearranged

explanation.surface: A child's wrestling bout where the top score might be won.
explanation.walkthrough: Shuffle the letters of TOP POINTS, take out those of TOTS, and the rest form the answer. The blog notes the score belongs to judo rather than wrestling.
explanation.definitionFit: An ippon is the full winning point in judo, the top score a contestant can get.

clue.text: Phelps heading off for training in pool? Not these days

indicators.note: training puts something through drills, reshaping it, so the letters are rearranged
the word's head, its first letter, comes off

parts.note: Michael Phelps, the US Olympic swimmer, taken as written

explanation.surface: The swimmer Phelps has stopped training in the pool these days.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Heading off' removes the first P of PHELPS to leave HELPS, which 'for training' rearranges.
explanation.definitionFit: Plesh is an obsolete Spenserian word for a pool or puddle, hence 'not these days'.

clue.text: E.g. Cava from Spain, only quite good, half filled with air inside?

parts.note: E is the international vehicle code for Spain

indicators.note: the piece goes inside the other word

parts.note: so-so means only middling
pumped means filled with air; half of that word is PUM

explanation.surface: Spanish cava, only fair, half of it fizz.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Half filled with air' means half of 'pumped'; 'inside' puts it within 'only quite good', giving SPUMOSO after Spain's code. The blog doubts pumped quite means filled with air.
explanation.definitionFit: Espumoso is the Spanish term for sparkling wine, and cava is a Spanish sparkling wine.

clue.text: Some Finns settled in USA (Americanized)

indicators.note: settled in means lodged inside, so the letters sit within these words

parts.note: the letters run across the end of USA and the start of Americanized

explanation.surface: A group of Finns emigrate to the USA and become Americans.
explanation.definitionFit: The Saame, or Sami, are the indigenous people of Lapland, living in northern Finland and its neighbours.

clue.text: Irritating experience with purgative, looking back — the young often get it

parts.note: a rub is an irritating difficulty, as in 'there's the rub'

indicators.note: looking back means read in reverse order

parts.note: aloes is a bitter purgative drug made from the aloe plant

explanation.surface: Taking a laxative is an unpleasant experience that children often have to go through.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Looking back' reverses the purgative, giving EOLA. The definition is a description, not a synonym: measles, which children often catch.
explanation.definitionFit: Rubeola is the medical name for measles, a disease common in childhood.

clue.text: Rail superintendent getting refurbished trams ready

indicators.note: refurbished means done up again, so the letters are reworked

explanation.surface: A railway manager has the renovated trams ready to go.
explanation.definitionFit: A yardmaster is a railway official in charge of a marshalling yard, a superintendent of rail operations.

clue.text: Ball's headed by Bowles maybe showing some of the old poetry

parts.note: Stan Bowles was an English footballer, so Bowles may be STAN
Zoe Ball is a British radio and TV presenter, so Ball's gives ZOE'S

explanation.surface: A football match where the ball is headed by a player called Bowles.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Headed by' puts STAN first. Stan Bowles was a QPR and England footballer, and Zoe Ball a BBC presenter.
explanation.definitionFit: Stanzoes is an old plural of stanza, the verses into which a poem is divided.

clue.text: The old venerate former king (name lost)

indicators.note: the letter for name is lost from the word

parts.note: Henry was the name of eight English kings

explanation.surface: Old subjects revering a king whose name has been forgotten.
explanation.definitionFit: Hery is an obsolete Spenserian verb meaning to praise or honour, hence an archaic word for venerate.
